name: maxima
why: A computer algebra system descended from MIT's Macsyma, with symbolic math that rewards a long afternoon of exploration.

brief.what_it_is: Maxima is a computer algebra system for manipulating symbolic and numerical expressions. The homepage lists differentiation, integration, Taylor series, Laplace transforms, ordinary differential equations, systems of linear equations, polynomials, sets, lists, vectors, matrices and tensors. It takes expressions typed at a prompt and returns symbolic or numerical results, using exact fractions, arbitrary-precision integers and variable-precision floating-point numbers. It can also plot functions and data in two and three dimensions. The plain maxima program runs in a terminal, and the wxMaxima and XMaxima front ends (included in the downloads) provide a notebook interface with formatted math output.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage frames it as a free, open-source descendant of MIT's Macsyma, the late-1960s computer algebra system, and says it is the only system based on that effort still publicly available with an active user community. Its history section credits William Schelter, who maintained the Maxima branch from 1982 until his death in 2001 and in 1998 obtained permission to release the source under the GPL, with a user and developer group carrying it on since.
brief.install_notes: The homepage says Maxima installs on Windows, Linux and Mac, with detailed instructions for each, and that full source is available via git. The wxMaxima and XMaxima front ends come in the downloads. I did not open the Installation page, so anything beyond that (runtimes, Lisp requirements, first-run steps) is unverified. The brew formula lists three executables: maxima, rmaxima and xmaxima.
brief.standout: It is a direct line of descent from Macsyma, and the homepage says many later systems such as Maple and Mathematica were inspired by it. It is GPL-licensed and still actively developed, which is unusual for a CAS of its age.
brief.status: Maintained, by the homepage's own account. It says Maxima 'is updated very frequently', and the page footer shows a last modification of 2026/03/01 23:11:36 UTC. That date is the website's, not a software release date, and I did not check the versions page or the git log.
brief.caveats: The homepage does not say which platforms or features are missing. The plain maxima program is a terminal tool, so the notebook experience depends on wxMaxima or XMaxima. The brew caveats field is empty. I did not open the documentation or installation pages, so build details are unknown.

entry.title: Maxima
entry.tldr: A free computer algebra system descended from MIT's 1960s Macsyma: type an expression, get exact symbolic answers for calculus, algebra and more.
entry.deeper_look:
Maxima manipulates mathematical expressions as symbols rather than just numbers. The homepage lists differentiation, integration, Taylor series, Laplace transforms, ordinary differential equations, systems of linear equations, polynomials, sets, lists, vectors, matrices and tensors. It uses exact fractions, arbitrary-precision integers and variable-precision floats, so results stay exact until you ask for a number. It can also plot functions and data in two and three dimensions.

The plain `maxima` program is a terminal prompt. You type an expression and it returns a simplified, symbolic or numerical result. Graphical front ends, wxMaxima and XMaxima, give a notebook-style interface with formatted math output. The brew formula also installs `rmaxima` and `xmaxima`.

The history is the interesting part. The homepage calls Maxima "a descendant of Macsyma, the legendary computer algebra system developed in the late 1960s at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology," and says many later systems, such as Maple and Mathematica, were inspired by that line of work. William Schelter maintained the Maxima branch from 1982 until his death in 2001. In 1998 he obtained permission to release the source under the GPL, and a user and developer group has carried it on since.

The idea underneath is that algebra and calculus can be done by a program that rewrites expressions by rule, the way you would on paper. Using it shows you what a computer algebra system does that a calculator cannot.
entry.install:
brew install maxima
# the formula pulls in sbcl (a Lisp), gnuplot, rlwrap and gettext

try_this.what_happens: Lists the command-line options for the terminal program.
Shows the options for the rlwrap-wrapped variant, which is meant to give line editing and history at the prompt.
Shows the options for the graphical XMaxima front end.

entry.whats_unique: It is a direct line of descent from Macsyma, the 1960s MIT system, and it is GPL-licensed and still developed. That is unusual for a computer algebra system this old.
entry.caveats: The plain maxima program is terminal-only, so the notebook experience depends on wxMaxima or XMaxima, and the brief did not check the documentation or install details.
